metadata.name: grep
metadata.displayName: grep - Search text patterns in files
metadata.description: Search for patterns in files using regular expressions

installation.note: grep is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: grep (global regular expression print) searches for patterns in files or input streams. It's one of the most powerful and commonly used text processing tools, capable of finding lines matching regular expressions. It's essential for log analysis, code searching, and text filtering.
when_to_use: Search for specific text in files

syntax.description: Search for PATTERN in FILE(s). If no files are specified, grep reads from standard input. PATTERN can be a simple string or a regular expression.

misconceptions.title: grep only works with files
misconceptions.misconception: grep can only search in files
misconceptions.reality: grep can search in files, but also reads from standard input. You can pipe output to grep: ps aux | grep firefox
misconceptions.tip: grep works great with pipes - many commands pipe to grep for filtering: ls -la | grep txt

misconceptions.title: grep is case-sensitive only
misconceptions.misconception: grep always requires exact case matching
misconceptions.reality: By default grep is case-sensitive, but use -i flag for case-insensitive searches. This is often needed.
misconceptions.tip: Always consider using -i when searching user-generated content or logs where capitalization may vary

common_pitfalls.issue: Not escaping special characters in patterns
common_pitfalls.description: Special regex characters like . * + need escaping when searching for literal characters
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -F for fixed strings (no regex), or escape special characters: grep '\+.*' (to search for literal + and .)

common_pitfalls.description: grep can match binary content and show garbled output
common_pitfalls.solution: Use grep -I to skip binary files, or --text to force text mode. Check file type first with file command.

common_pitfalls.description: grep -r can be slow on large directory trees
common_pitfalls.solution: Use --exclude-dir to skip directories (like .git, node_modules). Or use find with -exec grep for more control.

common_pitfalls.issue: Not using word boundaries for exact matches
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -w for whole word matches, or use regex word boundaries: grep '\berror\b'

best_practices: Use -i for case-insensitive searches when case might vary
Use -n to show line numbers - essential for large files
Use -r for recursive searches in directories
Use -w for whole word matches to avoid partial matches
Use -E for extended regex when using OR (|) or other advanced patterns
Use -l to find which files contain matches (faster than showing all matches)
Use -c to count matches instead of displaying them
Use -v to filter out unwanted lines
Combine with pipes: ps aux | grep firefox
Use --exclude-dir to skip directories in recursive searches
performance_tips: grep is very fast for text search
Use --exclude-dir for recursive searches to skip large directories (.git, node_modules)
Use -F for fixed strings (no regex) - faster than regex matching
For very large files, grep might be slower - consider splitting files first
Use grep -l first to find files, then grep specific files if needed

additional_notes.regex_support: grep supports regular expressions - use -E for extended regex, or -P for Perl-compatible regex (if available)
additional_notes.piping: grep works great with pipes - many commands pipe output to grep for filtering
additional_notes.binary_files: Be careful with binary files - use -I to skip them or --text to force text mode
additional_notes.color_output: grep usually highlights matches in color (if terminal supports). Use --color=always for pipes, --color=never to disable
additional_notes.fixed_strings: Use -F or fgrep for fixed string search (no regex interpretation) - faster and safer for literal strings
